newsitem.title: USA: U.S. base metals premiums steady, activity subdued.
newsitem.headline: U.S. base metals premiums steady, activity subdued.

text.p: Base metals premiums in the United States remain relatively steady but spot activity was still subdued as the market left the traditional holiday period behind, traders said.

After the heady gains in aluminum premiums in the past two months, the market has consolidated much of the gains, but slipping some 0.25 cent in the past week to 5.00 to 5.25 cents per pound over LME cash.

The Midwest alloy market was firm, holding on to recent gains in its bid to bridge the gap with recent scrap price hikes. Benchmark A380 alloy was quoted at 74 to 75 cents per pound, with the top end of the range looking firm.
Scrap was partly tight because some of the Russian secondary aluminum, used as feed instead of scrap by some smelters, was going to Japan instead of the U.S., a Midwest aluminum official said.
Lead premiums have slipped a touch, down about half a cent to 2.50 to 3.00 cents per pound, as the winter auto battery-making season grinds to a halt.
"The cold weather in the Midwest kept the market propped up a bit, but the battery season is basically over," industry consultant David Cook of Lake Engineering said.
Nickel premiums were largely unchanged at 8.00 to 10.00 cents according to most traders.
A scrap merchant said some stainless mills have settled their February contracts at $800 a gross ton, up from about $735 in January.
The hike was simply due to stronger LME nickel prices and represented no real increase. "There is plenty of scrap out there," the merchant said.

Premiums on nickel offers for 241 tonnes to the U.S. Mint this week were very high at 14 to 15 cents, puzzling some traders, though others said the deals should not be considered typical of the market.
Tin premiums have slipped about a cent as spot business remained lackluster. "I don't see premiums collapsing - with the LME down at these levels, the premiums don't go lower," a merchant said.

Grade A tin premiums were quoted at 5.50 to 7.00 cents per pound over LME cash, compared to 6.00 to 8.00 cents last week. Low lead (50 ppm) tin was at 7.00 to 8.50 cents, down from 7.00 to 9.00 cents.
The low lead tin premium over Grade A metal has narrowed to such an extent that traders suggested some merchants may be willing to deliver the former in contracts signed for the latter.
Copper scrap merchants said business was quiet after the sharp fall in LME and COMEX cathode prices this week, prompting yards to hang on to material in the hope of a rebound in the market.
Some merchants suggested that a tightening of the scrap market may lend some support to copper futures by increasing demand for cathode, a repeat of what happened last year after the Sumitomo crash.
